extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing obviousness of patent claims (including evidentiary and doctrinal considerations) such as omission or modification of elements, changes in proportions or sequence, optimization, ranges, and rebuttal evidence like criticality or teaching away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element when the element's function is not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if the function of the element is not desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art reference teaches an element for a particular function but the claimed use/environment does not require that function (e.g., no freshwater environment), omitting that element may be an obvious modification. (Cases: Ex parte Wu; In re Larson; In re Kuhle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element with retention of the element's function indicates nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an element and retention of its function is an indicium of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claimed invention removes a prior-art element but preserves the element's function by another means (e.g., eliminating an intermediate layer but retaining its protective function through a different layer), that fact supports nonobviousness. (Case: In re Edge.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity (mechanical replacement) is not patentably distinguishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity which accomplished the same result is not sufficient to distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply adding a timer/solenoid or automating an existing manual operation—if it achieves the same result—is typically obvious. The analysis looks to whether the automation produces any new or unexpected result beyond known manual function. (Case: In re Venner.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size/proportion alone are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere scaling up or recitation of relative dimensions is not sufficient to patentably distinguish over the prior art unless the claimed size/proportion causes different performance or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to larger size, or mere scaling of a prior art process/device, are generally obvious absent evidence that the change produces a new or unexpected result. (Cases: In re Rose; In re Rinehart; Gardner v. TEC Syst., Inc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape are often a matter of design choice and thus obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Configuration or shape of a product is generally an obvious matter of choice unless there is persuasive evidence that the particular configuration is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed shape/configuration does not yield a demonstrable and unexpected advantage, a person of ordinary skill would find it obvious. (Case: In re Dailey.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence of adding ingredients (reordering steps) are prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps or mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversing the order of coating vs impregnating, or choosing a different mixing order, will generally be obvious unless the change yields an unexpected effect. (Cases: Ex parte Rubin; In re Burhans; In re Gibson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a device portable does not alone confer patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact that a claimed device is portable or movable is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over an otherwise old device unless there are new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portability must produce some non-obvious functional advantage or unexpected result to overcome obviousness. (Case: In re Lindberg.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Making parts integral (one-piece construction) is an obvious engineering choice absent unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a one-piece (integral) construction for a multi-piece assembly is typically an obvious engineering choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-piece construction must produce an advantage contrary to the understandings and expectations of the art (e.g., eliminate need for dampening) to be nonobvious. (Cases: In re Larson; Schenck v. Nortron Corp. as contrast where integral structure was patentable due to unexpected advantage.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a part separable/removable is obvious if access or desirability suggests it
rubrics_metrics.description: If access to a feature would be desirable, making a previously fixed part removable (separable) is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converting a press-fit cap to a manually removable cap would be obvious where access is desired for a known purpose. (Case: In re Dulberg.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a device adjustable is not patentable absent inventive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustability, where needed and recognized in the art, is not a patentable advance and substitutions providing adjustability are obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the art recognizes the need for adjustment, substituting joints or mechanisms to allow adjustability (e.g., universal joint) is obvious unless it yields unexpected results. (Case: In re Stevens.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Making an operation continuous instead of batch is generally obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring continuous addition or continuous operation where the prior art uses batch operation is normally obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converting batch processing to continuous processing will be obvious absent evidence of unexpected results produced by continuous operation. (Case: In re Dilnot.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of parts (changing direction or which part moves) is obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply reversing which part moves or the direction of a part's movement is an obvious modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reversal does not change operation or produce an unexpected result, it is an obvious design choice. (Case: In re Gazda.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of parts lacks patentable significance absent new or unexpected result
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere duplication of parts does not confer patentability unless the duplication produces a new and unexpected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding additional ribs, elements, or duplicating structures is obvious unless demonstrably producing a distinct functional advantage. (Case: In re Harza.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement of parts is obvious absent change in operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting position or rearranging parts is obvious if it does not modify the device's operation or produce unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing placement of a switch or contact is typically an obvious matter of design choice. (Cases: In re Japikse; In re Kuhle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying an old product is not inherently nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Purer forms of known products may be patentable, but mere purity by itself does not render the product nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the purified form has the same utility as prior forms, whether prior art suggests the form or methods to obtain it, and whether the purified product has structural/functional differences. Product-by-process improvements that only increase purity without structural/functional differences generally do not confer patentability. (Cases: In re Bergstrom; In re Cofer; Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma; Ex parte Stern.) See MPEP § 2113 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping, approaching, or similar ranges/amounts/proportions give rise to prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie inside prior art ranges (or are merely close), a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlapping endpoints, numerically close values, or ranges disclosed across multiple references can establish a prima facie case unless applicant shows criticality or unexpected results. Considerations include whether the prior art range is so broad as to be a genus, and whether the prior art teaches a preference leading away from the claimed species. (Cases: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff; In re Geisler; Titanium Metals v. Banner; In re Peterson; others.) See MPEP § 2131.03 and §§ 2144.x references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine optimization within prior art conditions is not inventive absent criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in concentrations, temperatures, or other parameters reached by routine experimentation will not support patentability unless there is evidence these parameters are critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where general conditions are disclosed in prior art, discovering optimum or workable ranges by routine methods is not inventive. Examiners should look for evidence of criticality or unexpected results (e.g., improved properties) to overcome routine optimization. (Cases: In re Aller; Peterson; In re Hoeschele; Merck v. Biocraft; In re Kulling; In re Geisler; KSR v. Teleflex.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections based on routine optimization must include an articulated rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly support a rejection based on routine optimization, the examiner must make findings of relevant facts and present underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail explaining why it would have been routine to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusory assertion of 'common sense' or 'intuitive' is insufficient; the articulated rationale should explain the motivation and reasonable expectation of success (see In re Stepan; In re Van Os; Arendi v. Apple). 'Obvious to try' can be a valid rationale post-KSR when there is a design need/market demand and a finite number of predictable solutions, but prior to relying on 'obvious to try' the parameter must be recognized as a result-effective variable in some contexts (see In re Antonie; KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — showing that a claimed range is critical (unexpected results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness by showing the criticality of the claimed range, typically by demonstrating that the claimed range achieves unexpected results relative to the prior art range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant bears the burden to establish criticality with proper factual showings. A change in degree must produce a difference in kind (a new property) rather than just a quantitative improvement. (Cases: In re Woodruff; Minerals Separation v. Hyde; In re Scherl; In re Becket; In re Lilienfeld; In re Wells; E.I. DuPont v. Synvina; UCB v. Actavis.) See MPEP §§ 716.02–716.02(g) for discussion of criticality and unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — showing that the prior art teaches away from the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the prior art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching away is particularly strong evidence of nonobviousness where prior art undermines the motivation for combination. Courts evaluate whether the art's teachings would have discouraged a person of ordinary skill from the claimed path. (Cases: U.S. v. Adams; Depuy Spine v. Medtronic; Allergan v. Sandoz; discussion in In re Geisler where purported teaching away was found insufficient.)
